result:
The first thing that comes is the wind. Not a breeze, not a metaphor, but actual wind, the kind that arrives before you’re ready and rearranges everything you thought was nailed down. It’s 3:17 a.m. in whatever city this is, and the curtains are arguing with the window frame like two old lovers who know exactly which buttons still work. I’m sitting here with cold coffee and the kind of silence that has weight.

I keep thinking about how every person I’ve ever loved left fingerprints on me that I can’t scrub off. Not scars, exactly. More like invisible tattoos that only show up under certain light. My mother’s laugh lives somewhere behind my left ear. An ex-girlfriend’s way of saying “you’re an idiot” still echoes in the hollow of my throat when I’m about to say something reckless. We are all just walking around carrying other people’s weather.

There’s a spider in the corner of the room that’s been building the same web for three days. Every night I knock it down with a broom and every morning it’s back, more intricate, more defiant. I’ve started to respect it. Tenacity has a certain holiness when you’re running on three hours of sleep and the vague suspicion that you’re disappointing several versions of your younger self simultaneously.

I wonder what the spider thinks of me. Probably that I’m a chaotic god. One moment benevolent enough to leave the lights on so it can hunt, the next moment a destructive force that obliterates weeks of work with one swing. The universe must look at us the same way. We’re all just trying to build something beautiful in corners while larger forces occasionally wreck everything for reasons that must seem arbitrary from our level.

Sometimes I talk to the moon like it’s an old friend who owes me money. “You saw everything,” I tell it. “You watched me cry in that parking lot in 2017 and you didn’t even blink.” The moon never answers but that’s okay. Some relationships thrive on one-sided conversations. My therapist says this is displacement. I say it’s cheaper than actually calling the people I should probably call.

I’ve been collecting almost-memories lately. The way my grandfather smelled like sawdust and wintergreen. How my sister used to fall asleep during movies and wake up convinced she’d seen the whole thing. The exact sound my father made clearing his throat before telling me he was proud of me (which only happened twice, both times while he was looking at something else). These aren’t stories with beginnings and ends. They’re more like stones I keep in my pocket that I take out and worry between my fingers when the world gets too loud.

The coffee is completely undrinkable now. It tastes like regret and burnt dreams, which feels appropriate. I should make more but that would require standing up and I’m not sure my legs remember how to be legs. They’ve been pretending to be roots for the past hour, trying to burrow through the floorboards and find some stability down there in the dark.

I keep almost writing about love but then I don’t. Love is the word we use when we’re trying to explain why we let certain people destroy us beautifully. It’s the excuse and the crime and the forgiveness all at once. I’ve been in love with at least seven people who never existed and three who did but only in passing. The barista who drew a tiny dragon on my cup every Tuesday for six months. The woman on the train who cried at her own reflection. The version of myself I was supposed to become that I murdered quietly sometime around 2009.

There’s a bird outside that’s either dying or singing about it. Hard to tell the difference sometimes. Both sound like they’re trying to claw their way out of something. I relate.

I’ve started measuring time in almosts. The almost-apologies I never sent. The almost-cities I almost moved to. The almost-person I almost became before fear put its gentle hand on my shoulder and suggested we stay where it’s familiar. Familiar is just another word for slowly dying in ways that feel like living.

The spider has given up on the corner and is now attempting to build across my laptop screen. This feels like a sign. Or performance art. Or both. I’m trying to decide if I should let it. There’s something perfect about a spiderweb stretched across words, like nature saying, “Yes, but have you considered stillness?”

My hands are cold. My thoughts are loud. The night is stretching itself thin trying to reach morning. I’m 1,000 words deep into whatever this is and I still don’t know what I’m trying to say except maybe this:

We are all spiders and wind and almost-memories and cold coffee. We are all trying to build something in the corners while larger forces rearrange us. We are all carrying other people’s weather and wondering if the moon remembers our worst nights.

And somehow, against all odds, we keep singing like dying birds. We keep swinging brooms at our own webs. We keep loving people who become ghosts and ghosts who feel like people. We keep going.

The spider just walked across the word “hope” on my screen.

I’m going to let it stay.
